name: no-time
title: No Time to Type
kicker: Why this talk · the second ground has four legs
html:
No Time to Type

Have you ever tried to write code with a leash in one hand? I don’t recommend it.

Half the Answer: /remote-control

The session runs on my machine. I steer it mostly by dictating into my phone.

The Other Half: Rigor Without Watching

BDD for real, the same way every time: Gherkin, red, code, green, commit.

Asking Nicely? Probably Not.

Instructions are advisory, so hooks enforce the order. I read the record afterward.

Notice that an agent calling an API needs the same thing: controls that still hold when nobody is watching. hooks.json

/remote-control

Please give me an update

Red run logged. Writing the fix.

How’s it going?

Green. Commit gate: TDD order checked.

🐕 pulling. back in 20

Illustrative, not a transcript. The two questions are the real ones, every evening. So is the dog.
say: Have you ever tried to write code with a leash in one hand? I don't recommend it. Between family and a new dog, the time I used to spend at a keyboard is gone. Half of the answer was Claude Code's /remote-control. The session runs on my machine, and I steer it mostly by speech-to-text dictation into my phone, from wherever I am. Most evenings I send two messages: 'Please give me an update' and 'How's it going?' Fair enough, but that's only half. An agent I can't watch needs the three R's before anyone else's does: it has to follow BDD for real, and it has to do that the same way every time: Gherkin first, a red run, the code, a green run, and only then a commit. Can you get that by asking nicely? Probably not. Instructions to a model are advisory. So hooks enforce the order: a write out of turn is refused, every run is logged, and the commit gate checks the order before anything lands. I don't watch the agent; I read the record afterward. Notice that this is exactly what an agent calling an API needs, too: controls that still hold when nobody is watching. So how do you trust code you didn't watch being written? That's the bdd-gates skill.

deck:ref.name: right-behavior
deck:ref.label: RIGHT-BEHAVIOR
deck:ref.title: Right behavior: only what the state allows, and a reason when not
deck:ref.summary: The agent is offered only the acts the current state allows, sends each one with the validator from the state it read, and gets a reason when an act is absent. At the small scale it is a Gherkin scenario that says what right means before any code is written.

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.

deck:ref.label: NO-TIME
deck:ref.title: No time to type
deck:ref.summary: Family and a new dog took the typing time: one hand on a leash, a phone in the other. Half the fix is Claude Code's /remote-control: the session runs on my machine, steered mostly by speech-to-text dictation. The other half is rigour without watching: the agent must behave the same way every time and follow BDD strictly (Gherkin, red, code, green, commit), so hooks enforce the order and log every run, and the record is read later instead of the agent being monitored. Controls that hold while nobody watches: what this talk asks of agents calling APIs too.
